source: Talhelm, Zhang, Oishi et al. (2024) People quasi-randomly assigned to farm rice are more collectivistic than people assigned to farm wheat. Nature Communications
finding: Natural experiment: two state farms 56 km apart, one rice (Lianhu) one wheat (Qukou), staff assigned by the government. Rice farmers were less individualist, more loyal to a friend over a stranger, and more holistic on a triad task, after controlling for demographics.
numbers: Triad (holistic) task: B=0.28, t(181)=2.24, p=.025, 95% CI [0.04,0.53], r=.15 (N=188 on thought task). Loyalty/nepotism B=1.83, t(189)=2.63, p=.009, r=.18. Self-inflation (family) B=-1.92, t(189)=-2.62, p=.010, r=.18; with friends B=-0.65, p=.377 (ns). Rice farmers chose about 90% relational pairings vs about 75% Chinese students and 60% US students in earlier work. Loyalty gap USD 24 vs USD 50 East-West; self-inflation gap about two-thirds of UK-Japan gap.
limits: Quasi-random, not true randomisation; two farms only (one rice, one wheat), so farm-specific factors cannot be separated from crop. Not probability sampling. Same lab as the original rice theory. Effects small (r .15-.18). Age strongly related to holism (B=0.07, p<.001).
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed: one causal-leaning design supports the rice effect at about half the East-West size. For the agent: a crop or region label predicts style only weakly; do not let a culture tag override item-level evidence.
quote: These results rule out confounds in tests of the rice theory, such as temperature, latitude, and historical events.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across sample and setting (preprint full text), item 20: Norenzayan, Smith, Kim & Nisbett (2002) Study 2
finding: The Norenzayan 2002 Study 2 item replicated in the instruction effect (rules under 'belong to', family resemblance under 'similar to') and the effect was larger than the original. The predicted WEIRD advantage in rule use appeared only under 'belong to' and reversed under 'similar to'.
numbers: Original Study 2: 52 European American, 52 Asian American, 53 East Asian (N=157). Under 'belong to' EA 69%, East Asian 70% rule-based. Under 'similar to' EA 69% rule (d=1.65), East Asian 41% rule (d=-0.93), Asian American 46%. Preregistered contrast belong-vs-similar: original EA d=0.00, East Asian d=0.67. Replication N=7,396: belong 64% rule, similar 44% rule, t(7,227.59)=37.05, d=0.86, 95% CI [0.81,0.91]. WEIRD vs less WEIRD: belong 65.2 vs 59.8% rule; similar 42.8 vs 48.4% rule. Order moderation d=0.05.
limits: The pooled preregistered test is of the instruction effect, not of East Asian vs European American. WEIRD split is a binary exploratory label, not continuous cultural distance. Item is Study 2, not Study 1. The instruction effect is large in every group (d about 0.9).
agent_relevance: Gap 3 closed in part. Gap 10 answered for Study 2 only (N=157); Study 1 still unread. The instruction (belong vs similar) moves answers far more than culture does; for the agent, wording of the question is a bigger lever than any assumed cultural style.
quote: participants asked which group the target belongs to were more likely to classify based on a rule

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2, overall results and moderation by WEIRD (preprint full text)
finding: Across 28 effects, variation across sites came more from the effect studied than from site. Exploratory WEIRD vs less WEIRD moderation was small.
numbers: Median original d=0.60 vs replication d=0.15. 21 of 28 pooled effects smaller than original WEIRD finding, 7 larger. 16 (57%) replications d<.20; 9 (32%) opposite direction. Q heterogeneity significant in 11 (39%); only one effect Tau>0.20; nine Tau near or above 0.10. Effects positive in aggregate were significant in only 11-46% of individual samples.
limits: WEIRD was a binary split; no continuous cultural-distance model in this text (searched for 'continuous' and 'cultural distance': no relevant hit). Sites are mostly university samples, often culturally close to WEIRD.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 second half: continuous-distance test not found; stays open. A single-site significant result in a cross-cultural claim is weak evidence.

source: Mercier, Zhang, Qu, Lu & Van der Henst (2015) Do Easterners and Westerners treat contradiction differently? J Cognition and Culture 15
finding: Abstract (via Crossref): two Peng and Nisbett (1999) experiments retested with alternative interpretations plus a new third test; Chinese and French participants behaved similarly, with no cross-cultural difference.
numbers: N and effect sizes NOT obtained: SSRN and publisher pages blocked. Correction: Crossref author list is Mercier, Zhang, Qu, Lu, Van der Henst; earlier line b15 listed Yama.
limits: Abstract only. Comparison group is French, not American. Original-authors reply not found.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for numbers. Still lowers weight on 'Easterners accept contradiction' as a reasoning style.

source: Atari, Xue, Park, Blasi & Henrich (2023) Which Humans? (PsyArXiv full text, version of 22 Sep 2023)
finding: Atari ran a Nisbett-style triad task on GPT and compared it with human data from 31 populations that took the identical online triad task (yourmorals.org). GPT 'thinks' like WEIRD people, closest to the Netherlands, Finland, Sweden, Ireland.
numbers: GPT queried 1,100 times with 20 triads (prompt: which two of the three are most closely related). Humans: 31 populations (Mapuche by interview, different version). Survey part: 65 national samples, 262 variables, 1,000 GPT samples per question; GPT-human similarity vs cultural distance from US r=-.70 (Spearman -.72); correlations with development indices .85, .85, .69. Closest to US and Uruguay, then Canada, N. Ireland, NZ, GB, Australia, Andorra, Germany, Netherlands; farthest Ethiopia, Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan.
limits: Preprint. Model version not stated in main text (ChatGPT/GPT, GPT-3.5 era). The triad score for GPT is only in a figure; no exact holism percentage or CI in text. Text version of the triad task was rephrased. Only the triad task, not change blindness or contradiction.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 6 closed in part: a Nisbett task with at least 1,100 runs and same-platform human data does exist (triad). It shows WEIRD alignment on a reasoning-style task as well as on values. K19 (no study found) is revised.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov & Suhr (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design (FormatSpread). ICLR
finding: Meaning-preserving prompt formatting changes alter benchmark accuracy a lot, even with larger models, more examples, or instruction tuning; format performance only weakly correlates between models.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points spread for LLaMA-2-13B; median spread 7.5 points across tasks; about 10 points on average over 50+ tasks; 20% of tasks consistently above 9-point spreads for LLaMA-2 and Falcon settings (some above 70). GPT-3.5 across 320 formats: up to 56 points, median spread 6.4.
limits: Few-shot, mostly classification-style tasks and open models; not chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks. Equal-token control not reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 closed in part: prompt-form variance is also large on standard benchmarks (several to tens of points), consistent with Sun and Wang eta2=0.54. Report ranges over wording, never one wording, when judging style or culture effects.

source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee & Jurgens (2024) When 'a helpful assistant' is not really helpful: personas in system prompts do not improve performance
finding: 162 personas (6 relationship types, 8 expertise domains) in system prompts did not improve accuracy on MMLU-based factual questions versus a no-persona control; effects were mostly random and the best persona per question could not be picked reliably.
numbers: 2,410 questions, 4 model families (six models incl. Llama3-70B, Qwen2.5-7B/72B, Mistral, FLAN-T5-11B). No persona statistically better than control. Qwen2.5-7B and 72B insensitive to all 162 personas; more personas hurt Llama3-70B. In-domain role coefficient 0.004 (p<.01). Audience prompts slightly better than speaker prompts, small effect.
limits: MMLU-style factual questions, not cultural personas and not logic or ARC. Selecting the best persona was near random.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 closed in part: persona prompts do not lift accuracy; a culture persona should not be expected to either. Do not add personas to the scaffold (SCHEMA 4b).

source: Kong et al. (2024) Better zero-shot reasoning with role-play prompting. NAACL
finding: Counter-evidence: a designed two-turn role-play prompt (e.g. math teacher) raised zero-shot reasoning accuracy over plain zero-shot across most of 12 reasoning benchmarks with ChatGPT.
numbers: AQuA 53.5% to 63.8%; Last Letter 23.8% to 84.2% (ChatGPT). Gain on AQuA varied with role wording (Table 4).
limits: Compared with weak zero-shot baselines; benefit tied to eliciting chain of thought, which Zero-Shot-CoT also does; depends on role wording; one older model; no cultural roles.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: role prompts can help when they trigger step-by-step reasoning, so the gain is a CoT effect, not a cultural effect. Net: persona effects on reasoning are inconsistent (d08 vs d09).

source: Shi et al. (2023) Language models are multilingual chain-of-thought reasoners (MGSM). ICLR
finding: Question and reasoning language changes math accuracy only modestly for PaLM-540B; English-pivot reasoning is competitive with native-language reasoning.
numbers: MGSM: 250 GSM8K problems translated into 10 languages. Average accuracy for four under-resourced languages 44.9% vs 47.9% for six high-resource languages (3-point gap). Thai, Telugu, Bengali on par with French, Japanese, Chinese. English CoT is a strong baseline.
limits: 2022, one model family; arithmetic problems with little cultural content; not a test of cultural style.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: reasoning accuracy survives language changes; values change more than math (see AlKhamissi in K15). Supports a language-neutral reasoning core.

source: Hu, Peng, Zhao, Qiu, Hung & Peng (2026) Machine culture as an emergent phenomenon in LLMs (re-read for RLHF mechanism)
finding: Model origin did not predict cultural alignment. The explanation offered for hyper-positive, zero-variance affect answers is RLHF 'service persona' plus training-data mode collapse, but this is a hypothesis, not an ablation.
numbers: Chinese model with English prompts on Ideal Low Arousal Positive affect: mean 5.00, SD 0.00, 100% ceiling. Paper cites alignment-tax and distributional-collapse literature as support.
limits: No base-vs-RLHF comparison and no data ablation; authors are in the Nisbett lineage (Peng).
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: no ablation separating RLHF from data. Treat the RLHF story as unproven; authors are interested parties.

source: Sabir, Gasper, Loem & Sharma (2025) Contrasting cognitive styles in vision-language models: holistic attention in Japanese vs analytical focus in English
finding: VLM captions are mostly analytic. Japanese prompts and Japanese image data raise the holistic share, and a model trained on Japanese (VILA-JP) was less holistic than GPT-4o-JP, which suggests pretraining setup matters more than prompt language alone.
numbers: 6-shot English captions on COCO: holistic 24.30% (GPT-4V), 26.20% (GPT-4o), 23.20% (LLaVA-CoT-11B), 19.30% and 19.20% (Gemma-3 12B and 27B). GPT-4o-JP 26.10% holistic on COCO. Back-translation shifts the ratio by an average of 13.21%.
limits: Caption holism is labelled by another model; counts are confounded by caption length; image data content changes the ratio.
agent_relevance: Gap 7, data side: data content and model, not language alone, move style. Still no RLHF ablation.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models, like humans, show content effects on reasoning tasks. PNAS Nexus (human sample details from methods)
finding: Human data for belief bias and content effects came only from UK English-first-language online participants. No non-Western humans were tested.
numbers: Humans: first 625 participants, plus 360 more with a bonus for the Wason task (total 985). 5-minute limit per question; 2023 online platform; UK only. Tasks: NLI, syllogisms, Wason. Models: Chinchilla, PaLM 2-M, PaLM 2-L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5.
limits: No cross-cultural human comparison; Western-only. Equal-token control not reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open for non-Western humans and for equal tokens. Content effects can be called a shared human-model bias only for UK samples.

source: Tao et al. (2024) Cultural bias and cultural alignment of large language models. PNAS Nexus (RLHF passage re-read)
finding: The paper notes that GPT-3.5-turbo added RLHF and that GPT-4 reward signals may have mitigated cultural bias, but it reports no controlled comparison against a base model.

agent_relevance: Gap 7: no RLHF-vs-data ablation in Tao either.
